# Capability matrix

<!-- Generated by `isoloom docs --matrix` from what each target decides. Change a target or the tier list (`cargo xtask tiers record`), then regenerate. -->

What each target does with each spec field. Every cell is the target's own decision about a small lab that uses the field: ✓ generated, ✗ refused, – not applicable. The reasons follow the grid.

## Tiers

Tiers: 1 proven by real runs on every host OS it exists on, 2 generated and validated, 3 experimental.

## Why a target refuses

### `machines.*.app.image`

- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`: lowering: an image's filesystem can't be reproduced on a fresh VM

### `machines.*.app.build`

- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`: lowering: a Dockerfile builds a container only

### `machines.*.app.appliance`

- `kubernetes`, `hybrid`, `external`: capability `network-appliances`: machine `m` is a network appliance (`app.appliance`), which runs on the Docker targets
- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`: lowering: an appliance's packaging exists only as a container

### `machines.*.app.steps`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.command`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: its steps install services, but nothing keeps one running in a container
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.app.steps[].copy`

- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`, `external`: lowering: a `copy` step on a VM comes with the configuration backends (Phase 4); containers build it today

### `machines.*.app.steps[].packages`

- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`, `external`: lowering: a `packages` step on a VM comes with the configuration backends (Phase 4); containers build it today

### `machines.*.app.steps[].playbook`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.app.steps[] = reboot`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.command`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `external`: capability `machine-process`: machine `m` sets its own process (`command` or `healthcheck`): an existing host runs what it already runs, Isoloom starts nothing on it

### `machines.*.healthcheck`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `external`: capability `machine-process`: machine `m` sets its own process (`command` or `healthcheck`): an existing host runs what it already runs, Isoloom starts nothing on it

### `machines.*.setup`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.environment`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.environment.*.input`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.depends_on`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `w` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: DigitalOcean cloud-vm takes one machine on one network: a droplet joins one VPC, at a private address DigitalOcean picks, so other machines couldn't reach it at its spec address

### `machines.*.depends_on`

- `hybrid`: capability `vm-after-container`: VM `v` depends on container `c`: VMs start first in a hybrid environment, for now

### `machines.*.resources`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.privileged`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.sysctls`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.ulimits`

- `kubernetes`: capability `ulimits`: machine `m` sets `ulimits`: Kubernetes has no per-container process limits
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.dns`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: DigitalOcean cloud-vm takes one machine on one network: a droplet joins one VPC, at a private address DigitalOcean picks, so other machines couldn't reach it at its spec address

### `machines.*.count`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m-01` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: DigitalOcean cloud-vm takes one machine on one network: a droplet joins one VPC, at a private address DigitalOcean picks, so other machines couldn't reach it at its spec address

### `machines.*.access`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.networks`

- `vagrant/qemu`: provider: `m` is on 2 networks, and QEMU gives a VM one
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: DigitalOcean cloud-vm takes one machine on one network: a droplet joins one VPC, at a private address DigitalOcean picks, so other machines couldn't reach it at its spec address
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: machine `m` is on several networks: a Linode instance has one VPC interface

### `machines.*.networks.*`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`, `hybrid`: capability `container-more-addresses`: machine `m` has several addresses on `lan`: a container has one address per network (Docker and Kubernetes give an endpoint one IPv4 address); run it on a VM target (its `os`, and `app.steps` for an app)
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: machine `m` has several addresses on `lan`: a Droplet has one address on its VPC (DigitalOcean has no secondary private address; a reserved IP is public)
- `external`: capability `container-more-addresses`: machine `m` has several addresses on `lan`: an existing host keeps the addresses it has, which Isoloom doesn't change

### `machines.*.networks.*`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: its steps install services, but nothing keeps one running in a container
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: machine `m` has several addresses on `lan`: a Droplet has one address on its VPC (DigitalOcean has no secondary private address; a reserved IP is public)
- `external`: capability `container-more-addresses`: machine `m` has several addresses on `lan`: an existing host keeps the addresses it has, which Isoloom doesn't change

### `machines.*.aliases`

- `kubernetes`: capability `machine-aliases`: machine `aliases` (dotted DNS names) aren't Kubernetes Service names
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.ports.*.publish`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.ports.*.protocol = udp`

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

### `machines.*.rate_limit`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`, `hybrid`, `vagrant/*`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`, `external`: capability `rate-limit`: machine `m` sets a `rate_limit`, which this target doesn't apply yet (the proxmox target does, on its network devices)

### `machines.*.hardware.arch = arm64`

- `cloud-docker`: target: machine `m`: arm64 on a cloud VM comes later (Graviton instances and arm64 images)
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `esxi`: target: machine `m`: ESXi runs x86-64 VMs only
- `cloud-vm/aws`: cloud: machine `m`: arm64 on AWS comes later (Graviton instances and arm64 AMIs)
- `cloud-vm/azure`: cloud: machine `m`: arm64 on Azure comes later (Arm-based sizes and arm64 images)
- `cloud-vm/gcp`: cloud: machine `m`: arm64 on Google Cloud comes later (Arm-based machine types and arm64 images)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: machine `m`: arm64 on DigitalOcean comes later (it has no arm64 droplets)
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: machine `m`: arm64 on Linode comes later (it has no arm64 plans)
- `cloud-vm/oci`: cloud: machine `m`: arm64 on Oracle Cloud comes later (Ampere shapes and arm64 images)

### `machines.*.hardware.tpm = required`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: only a VM gives it: a container has no kernel or firmware of its own
- `vagrant/vmware_desktop`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's vmware_desktop provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/parallels`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's parallels provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/qemu`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's qemu provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's utm provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/vmware_esxi`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's vmware_esxi provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `esxi`: capability `tpm`: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`), which this target doesn't give (Vagrant on VirtualBox, libvirt or Hyper-V, Proxmox and the big clouds do)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): DigitalOcean gives none
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Linode gives none

### `machines.*.hardware.tpm = required`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: Windows has no container form in 1.0
- `vagrant/vmware_desktop`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's vmware_desktop provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/parallels`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's parallels provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/qemu`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's qemu provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's utm provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `vagrant/vmware_esxi`: provider: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`): Vagrant's vmware_esxi provider gives none (VirtualBox, libvirt and Hyper-V do)
- `esxi`: capability `tpm`: machine `m` asks for a virtual TPM (`hardware.tpm: required`), which this target doesn't give (Vagrant on VirtualBox, libvirt or Hyper-V, Proxmox and the big clouds do)
- `cloud-vm/aws`: cloud: machine `m`: a TPM on a Windows VM on AWS needs Amazon's NitroTPM images (TPM-Windows_Server-*), which come later
- `cloud-vm/gcp`: cloud: machine `m`: Windows on GCP comes later
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: DigitalOcean cloud-vm is Linux only so far
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: Linode cloud-vm is Linux only so far
- `cloud-vm/oci`: cloud: Oracle Cloud cloud-vm is Linux only so far

### `machines.*.hardware.gpus`

- `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `hybrid`: capability `container-gpus`: machine `m` asks for GPUs (`gpus`): its container runs on a VM Isoloom creates, which has no GPU (the `docker` and `kubernetes` targets give the host's)
- `vagrant/*`, `esxi`: capability `vm-gpus`: machine `m` asks for GPUs (`gpus`): Vagrant passes no GPU to a local VM (Proxmox and the cloud targets do)
- `proxmox`: target: machine `m`: Proxmox passes the server's GPUs by name: list them in `gpus.ids` (PCI addresses such as 0000:01:00.0, or resource mappings)
- `cloud-vm/oci`: cloud: machine `m`: GPUs on Oracle Cloud come later (its GPU shapes are fixed, not the flexible shape every machine has, and take images built for them)

### `machines.*.hardware.gpus.ids`

- `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `hybrid`: capability `container-gpus`: machine `m` asks for GPUs (`gpus`): its container runs on a VM Isoloom creates, which has no GPU (the `docker` and `kubernetes` targets give the host's)
- `kubernetes`: target: machine `m`: `gpus.ids`: Kubernetes' scheduler picks the GPUs; give a `count` instead
- `vagrant/*`, `esxi`: capability `vm-gpus`: machine `m` asks for GPUs (`gpus`): Vagrant passes no GPU to a local VM (Proxmox and the cloud targets do)
- `cloud-vm/aws`: cloud: machine `m`: a AWS VM's GPUs come with its instance type: give `gpus` as a count, not `all` or `ids`
- `cloud-vm/azure`: cloud: machine `m`: a Azure VM's GPUs come with its instance type: give `gpus` as a count, not `all` or `ids`
- `cloud-vm/gcp`: cloud: machine `m`: a Google Cloud VM's GPUs come with its instance type: give `gpus` as a count, not `all` or `ids`
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: machine `m`: a DigitalOcean VM's GPUs come with its instance type: give `gpus` as a count, not `all` or `ids`
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: machine `m`: a Linode VM's GPUs come with its instance type: give `gpus` as a count, not `all` or `ids`
- `cloud-vm/oci`: cloud: machine `m`: GPUs on Oracle Cloud come later (its GPU shapes are fixed, not the flexible shape every machine has, and take images built for them)

### `machines.*.hardware.devices`

- `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`, `hybrid`: capability `container-devices`: machine `m` is given host devices (`devices`): only a container on your own Docker host reaches them (the `docker` target), not one in a VM Isoloom creates or a Kubernetes pod
- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`: lowering: the host's devices go to a container on the host's own Docker; a VM has its own

### `machines.*.hardware.nested_virtualization`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: only a VM gives it: a container has no kernel or firmware of its own
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `esxi`: capability `nested-virtualization`: machine `m` runs VMs inside (`nested_virtualization`): this target's VMs can't nest (Vagrant, Proxmox, AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud can)
- `cloud-vm/azure`: cloud: machine `m`: nested virtualization (`nested_virtualization`) on Azure comes later (AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud have it)
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: machine `m`: nested virtualization (`nested_virtualization`) on DigitalOcean comes later (AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud have it)
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: machine `m`: nested virtualization (`nested_virtualization`) on Linode comes later (AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud have it)

### `machines.*.hardware.boot`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: only a VM gives it: a container has no kernel or firmware of its own
- `hybrid`, `cloud-vm/*`: capability `own-boot`: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): this target boots a VM from its image's own kernel and firmware; Vagrant's libvirt provider boots it
- `vagrant/virtualbox`: provider: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): Vagrant's virtualbox provider boots the box as it is; the libvirt provider boots it
- `vagrant/vmware_desktop`: provider: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): Vagrant's vmware_desktop provider boots the box as it is; the libvirt provider boots it
- `vagrant/hyperv`: provider: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): Vagrant's hyperv provider boots the box as it is; the libvirt provider boots it
- `vagrant/parallels`: provider: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): Vagrant's parallels provider boots the box as it is; the libvirt provider boots it
- `vagrant/qemu`: provider: machine `m` sets `hardware.boot.kernel`, `hardware.boot.initrd`, `hardware.boot.cmdline`: Vagrant's QEMU provider boots the box's disk through its own firmware (only `firmware_format` applies); the libvirt provider boots it
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `vagrant/vmware_esxi`: provider: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): Vagrant's vmware_esxi provider boots the box as it is; the libvirt provider boots it
- `proxmox`: target: machine `m` sets `hardware.boot.kernel`: Proxmox boots the VM's disk through its own firmware (`firmware`, `order` and `firmware_format` apply); Vagrant's libvirt provider boots it
- `esxi`: target: machine `m` sets `hardware.boot.kernel`: ESXi boots the VM's disk through its own firmware (`firmware` applies, as `boot_firmware`); Vagrant's libvirt provider boots it

### `machines.*.hardware.boot.firmware = uefi`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`: lowering: only a VM gives it: a container has no kernel or firmware of its own
- `hybrid`, `cloud-vm/*`: capability `own-boot`: machine `m` boots its own way (`hardware.boot`): this target boots a VM from its image's own kernel and firmware; Vagrant's libvirt provider boots it

### `networks.*.gateway`

- `kubernetes`: capability `gateways`: networks with a `gateway` machine on Kubernetes come later
- `hybrid`: capability `gateways`: networks with a `gateway` machine in hybrid environments come later
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `proxmox`: target: networks with a `gateway` machine on Proxmox come later
- `esxi`: target: networks with a `gateway` machine on ESXi come later
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: a DigitalOcean VPC has no route tables, so no traffic can be sent through a machine
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: a Linode VPC has no route tables, so no traffic can be sent through a machine

### `networks.*.tc`

- `kubernetes`: capability `traffic-control`: link impairment (`tc`) needs a router in the path; Kubernetes has none
- `vagrant/qemu`: provider: `isoloom-router` is on 2 networks, and QEMU gives a VM one
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `isoloom-router` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/aws`, `cloud-vm/azure`: cloud: link impairment (`tc`) needs a router in the path; the cloud's security groups have none
- `cloud-vm/gcp`: cloud: link impairment (`tc`) needs a router in the path; the cloud's firewall rules have none
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: DigitalOcean cloud-vm takes one machine on one network: a droplet joins one VPC, at a private address DigitalOcean picks, so other machines couldn't reach it at its spec address
- `cloud-vm/linode`, `cloud-vm/oci`: cloud: link impairment (`tc`) needs a router in the path; the cloud's firewalls have none

### `networks.*.mtu`

- `docker`, `hosted`, `docker-vm`, `cloud-docker`, `kubernetes`, `hybrid`, `vagrant/*`, `external`: capability `network-mtu`: network `lan` sets its `mtu`, which this target doesn't carry yet (the proxmox target does)
- `cloud-vm/aws`: cloud: network `lan` sets its `mtu`: AWS has no setting for a network's MTU
- `cloud-vm/azure`: cloud: network `lan` sets its `mtu`: Azure has no setting for a network's MTU
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: network `lan` sets its `mtu`: DigitalOcean has no setting for a network's MTU
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: network `lan` sets its `mtu`: Linode has no setting for a network's MTU
- `cloud-vm/oci`: cloud: network `lan` sets its `mtu`: Oracle Cloud has no setting for a network's MTU

### `networks.*.ipv6`

- `hybrid`: capability `ipv6`: network `lan` is IPv6 (`ipv6`), which this target's networks don't carry yet
- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)
- `cloud-vm/aws`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: an AWS VPC takes an Amazon-provided (or your own registered) IPv6 block, never one the spec picks
- `cloud-vm/gcp`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: Google Cloud assigns a VPC's internal IPv6 range itself (inside fd20::/20), so the spec's block can't be kept
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: DigitalOcean VPCs are IPv4 only (a droplet's IPv6 address is a public one)
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: a Linode VPC's IPv6 ranges are Linode's to assign, so the spec's block can't be kept

### `networks.*.ipv6.only = true`

- `hybrid`: capability `ipv6`: network `lan` is IPv6 (`ipv6`), which this target's networks don't carry yet
- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`, `cloud-vm/*`, `external`: capability `ipv6-only`: network `lan` is IPv6-only (`ipv6.only`): this target needs IPv4 on every network (its router, its set-up, its transport)

### `networks.*.ipv6.addresses = auto`

- `hybrid`: capability `ipv6`: network `lan` is IPv6 (`ipv6`), which this target's networks don't carry yet
- `vagrant/*`, `proxmox`, `esxi`: capability `ipv6-auto`: network `lan` leaves IPv6 addresses to the target (`ipv6.addresses: auto`), and nothing on this target hands them out: use `static`
- `cloud-vm/aws`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: an AWS VPC takes an Amazon-provided (or your own registered) IPv6 block, never one the spec picks
- `cloud-vm/azure`: cloud: network `lan` leaves IPv6 addresses to the target (`ipv6.addresses: auto`): Isoloom gives each Azure interface the address derived from the machine's octet, so use `static`
- `cloud-vm/gcp`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: Google Cloud assigns a VPC's internal IPv6 range itself (inside fd20::/20), so the spec's block can't be kept
- `cloud-vm/digitalocean`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: DigitalOcean VPCs are IPv4 only (a droplet's IPv6 address is a public one)
- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: network `lan` is IPv6: a Linode VPC's IPv6 ranges are Linode's to assign, so the spec's block can't be kept

- `vagrant/hyperv`: provider: network `home`: bridged networks under Vagrant's Hyper-V provider come later
- `vagrant/libvirt`: provider: network `home`: bridged networks under Vagrant's libvirt provider come later

- `vagrant/utm`: provider: `m` is on a network, and vagrant_utm gives a VM no private network (it only forwards ports)

- `cloud-vm/linode`: cloud: machine `m` is on several networks: a Linode instance has one VPC interface
